title: Rekeying vs. Replacing Locks After Moving into a New SF Home
description: Moving to a new San Francisco home? Learn whether rekeying or replacing your door locks makes the most sense for your security and budget.
intro: Getting the keys to a new San Francisco apartment or house is an exciting milestone. Whether you just bought a classic Victorian in the Haight or signed a lease on a modern condo in South of Market, securing your entry points should be at the top of your moving checklist. You never know how many copies of the old keys are still floating around with previous tenants, realtors, contractors, or neighbors. That brings up an important question: should you rekey your existing hardware or replace the locks entirely? Here is a clear guide to help you choose the right option for your new home.

sections.heading: Understanding the Difference: Rekeying vs. Replacing
paragraphs: Before deciding which path to take, it helps to understand what happens during each service. Both methods achieve the same primary goal: preventing old keys from opening your doors. However, the process, time involved, and hardware outcome are quite different.

Rekeying involves altering the internal mechanism of your current lock cylinder. A locksmith changes the arrangement of the tiny key pins inside so that the lock now aligns with a brand-new key configuration. The existing handle, lever, decorative trim, and outer deadbolt shell remain on the door, but all former keys become completely useless.

Replacing a lock means taking off the entire lock assembly—including the deadbolt cylinder, latch mechanism, strike plate, and exterior handles—and installing completely new hardware. This leaves you with entirely new physical components inside and out.

sections.heading: When Rekeying Is the Smarter Choice
paragraphs: In many residential moves across San Francisco, rekeying is the most efficient and practical solution. If your current door hardware is functioning smoothly, shows minimal wear, and provides solid protection, there is often no reason to discard it.

Rekeying is particularly popular in historic San Francisco neighborhoods like the Castro, Pacific Heights, or Alamo Square. Many of these classic Edwardian and Victorian homes feature custom vintage brass trim, ornamental mortise locks, or tailored entry hardware that matches the home's architectural character. Finding a modern replacement that fits those exact door dimensions without custom woodwork can be difficult. Rekeying allows you to preserve that original beauty while resetting your access control.
It is also an excellent option if you want all your exterior doors to open with a single key, provided the existing lock cylinders are made by the same manufacturer or share a compatible keyway.
bullets: Preserves original, historic, or high-end door hardware.
Provides total peace of mind by rendering all previous keys inactive.
Allows multiple entry locks to be keyed alike for everyday convenience.
Requires less structural adjustment to existing door frames.

sections.heading: When Full Lock Replacement Is Necessary
paragraphs: While rekeying works in many scenarios, there are specific situations where installing brand-new locks is the safer and more sensible choice for a newly occupied property.

If the existing locks are visibly worn out, loose, or sticky when you turn the key, rekeying will not fix the mechanical degradation inside. San Francisco weather can also take a heavy toll on hardware. In western neighborhoods like the Sunset or Richmond districts, persistent ocean fog and salty Pacific air frequently cause hidden internal corrosion and rust. If a lock mechanism feels gritty or hard to operate due to weather wear, replacing it with fresh, weather-resistant hardware is the best course of action.

You should also consider replacement if you want to upgrade your security features. Moving into an older home might mean inheriting basic builder-grade locks that lack modern drill protection or heavy-duty strike plates. Replacing them gives you the chance to install Grade 1 deadbolts or modern electronic keypads.
bullets: Existing lock shows internal rust, structural wear, or damage.
Hardware is mismatched across front, side, and rear doors.
You want to upgrade to high-security cylinders or smart keyless entry.
The lock mechanism sticks or fails to extend fully into the frame.

sections.heading: San Francisco Architectural Factors to Keep in Mind
paragraphs: San Francisco real estate presents several unique hardware challenges that homeowners and tenants should keep in mind during a move.

Older buildings in the city often experience subtle structural settling over decades. This can cause doors and frames to shift slightly, leading to misaligned deadbolts and latches. When securing a new place, simply changing the key might not be enough if the deadbolt pinches against the strike plate. A professional lock assessment ensures that the lock not only responds to your new key, but also throws smoothly without forcing the bolt.

For residents moving into multi-family apartment buildings or shared flats, check your building rules or consult your property management before modifying entrance locks. In many cases, apartment front doors can be rekeyed so that your private key opens your unit while retaining compatibility with shared entrance systems where appropriate.

paragraphs: Securing your entry points should never be left to guesswork when settling into a new home. faq.question: Can all entry locks on my new home be rekeyed to use the same key?
faq.answer: Yes, provided the lock cylinders are from the same brand or share matching keyway designs. If your front and back doors use incompatible brands, a locksmith can evaluate whether swapping internal cylinders or matching hardware sets makes sense.

faq.question: Is rekeying safe if the previous owner kept old key copies?
faq.answer: Yes, rekeying is completely safe. Once the internal pins inside the cylinder are changed to match a new key pattern, any key cut to the old pattern will no longer operate the lock.

faq.question: Should renters rekey or replace locks when moving into a San Francisco apartment?
faq.answer: Renters should always consult their lease agreement and landlord before altering door locks. In most cases, landlords allow locks to be rekeyed as long as a duplicate of the new key is provided for management access.
